claim: 4-HNE accumulates during L. monocytogenes infection in murine hepatocytes at 6 hours post-infection to levels similar to those observed with addition of 10 µM pure 4-HNE.
source: We found that at 6 hr post infection, 4-HNE adducts accumulate to a similar level as those observed with the addition of the pure compound (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by dot blot data showing 4-HNE adduct accumulation in infected hepatocytes compared to exogenous 4-HNE treatment

claim: In the spleen of mice infected with L. monocytogenes, the entire organ exhibited increased staining for 4-HNE protein conjugates at 48 hours post-infection.
source: In the spleen, however, bacteria were diffusely distributed throughout the organ and the entire spleen of infected mice exhibited increased staining for 4-HNE protein conjugates (Figure 1B–E).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data showing increased 4-HNE staining in infected spleen tissue

claim: In the liver of mice infected with L. monocytogenes, there was no change in the abundance of 4-HNE protein conjugates at 48 hours post-infection despite clear foci of infection.
source: Clear foci of infection were visible in the liver with no change in the abundance of 4-HNE protein conjugates (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data showing no change in 4-HNE staining in infected liver tissue

claim: 4-HNE conjugates within the spleen were not evenly distributed among all cells, with a subset of cells showing very dark and robust staining.
source: We observed that 4-HNE conjugates within the spleen were not evenly distributed among all cells. Most of the tissue exhibited diffuse and constant staining and a subset of cells showed very dark and robust staining for 4-HNE conjugates (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry images showing heterogeneous 4-HNE staining patterns

claim: 4-HNE causes intermediate cytotoxicity (apoptosis) in eukaryotic cells at concentrations of 5-40 µM and necrosis at higher concentrations (40-100 µM).
source: Electrophilic stress due to 4-HNE conjugation to proteins causes eukaryotic cells to undergo apoptosis following intermediate 4-HNE exposure (5–40 µM) and necrosis at higher concentrations (40–100 µM) (Dalleau et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature

claim: 4-HNE is believed to accumulate to significantly higher levels (0.3-5 mM) near and within membranes than in the cytoplasm due to its lipophilicity.
source: However, due to 4-HNE's lipophilicity it is believed to accumulate to significantly higher levels (0.3–5 mM) near and within membranes than what is typically considered cytotoxic (Zimniak, 2011; Esterbauer et al., 1991; Uchida, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: B. subtilis and F. novicida exhibit a 4-log reduction in CFU when exposed to 4-HNE.
source: We observed variability in survival, ranging from a 4-log reduction in CFU for B. subtilis and Francisella novicida
evidence: Supported by bacterial survival assay data shown in Figure 2A

claim: S. aureus exhibits a 2-log reduction in CFU when exposed to 4-HNE.
source: a 2-log reduction for Staphylococcus aureus
evidence: Supported by bacterial survival assay data shown in Figure 2A

claim: E. coli and P. aeruginosa exhibit a 1-log reduction in CFU when exposed to 4-HNE.
source: a 1-log reduction for Escherichia coli and Pseudomonas aeruginosa

claim: E. faecalis exhibits a half-log reduction in CFU when exposed to 4-HNE.
source: to a half-log reduction for Enterococcus faecalis

claim: L. monocytogenes exhibits less than a half-log reduction in CFU when exposed to up to 640 µM of 4-HNE.

evidence: Supported by bacterial survival assay data shown in Figure 2A

claim: L. monocytogenes exhibits a dose-dependent delay in growth with increased exposure to 4-HNE.
source: Although 4-HNE exhibited limited bactericidal activity toward this organism, we observed a dose-dependent delay in growth of L. monocytogenes with increased exposure to 4-HNE (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by growth curve data showing delayed growth at increasing 4-HNE concentrations

claim: 4-HNE penetrates the bacterial cell envelope of L. monocytogenes and impacts cytosolic proteins.
source: Dot blots of L. monocytogenes cell lysates from bacteria exposed to increasing concentrations of 4-HNE indicated an accumulation of 4-HNE-protein adducts that correlated with increased 4-HNE exposure (Figure 2C), establishing that this aldehyde penetrates the bacterial cell envelope and impacts cytosolic proteins.
evidence: Supported by dot blot data showing dose-dependent accumulation of 4-HNE protein adducts in bacterial lysates

claim: 4-HNE adduct accumulation in bacteria can result in protein misfolding and crosslink-induced aggregation.
source: 4-HNE adduct accumulation can result in protein misfolding and crosslink-induced aggregation.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of 4-HNE effects on proteins

claim: Eukaryotic cells clear 4-HNE damaged proteins through proteasome and autophagy-mediated pathways.

claim: Bacteria target damaged proteins for degradation through the proteases that comprise the heat shock response.

claim: The heat shock response in bacteria is primarily transcriptionally regulated.
